name: Medpill

lead: Medpill is a term from looksmaxxing forums, formed on the model of blackpill and redpill. In the threads where it appears it refers to the claim that Mediterranean or dark-featured men, with darker hair, eyes and skin tones, are attractive to women and outperform fairer Nordic-type features.

Members use it to point to anecdotes, such as a woman praising a tanned, dark-haired partner, and to argue that colouring matters in how people are perceived. It is a community claim rather than a researched concept.

paras: In practice it appears as forum threads sharing anecdotes and photographs. Members who accept the idea may talk about tanning, hair colour and darker-toned styling, though the term mostly functions as a discussion label.

The label is discussed in threads that mix appearance talk with ethnic generalisations, and attractiveness research reports that preferences vary by person and culture. It carries no direct physical risks; tanning has well-documented skin-cancer risk.

angle.text: Believers use the idea to reassess which of their features help them and, in some cases, to try tanning, darker hair or other colour styling. It is a way of thinking about presentation rather than a procedure, and the term is a community label rather than a researched concept.

lead: Medpill (also written med pill) is slang used on looksmax.org and related forums. In the threads where it appears, it denotes the belief that Mediterranean and dark-featured men, with darker hair, eyes and skin tone, are preferred by women over fairer, Nordic-type men [1].

The word follows the community's "pill" naming convention, which descends from the red and blue pills in the 1999 film The Matrix. The manosphere adopted red pill for a set of beliefs about gender, and incel forums developed black pill as a more fatalistic offshoot centred on physical attractiveness; further pills such as medpill borrow the format for a single claim that members present as a revelation [2][3].

People who take the idea seriously use it to reconsider which of their own features count in their favour, and some talk about tanning, hair colour, eye colour and darker styling. Published attractiveness research looks at neighbouring questions, such as skin colouration, hair colour and tanning, and generally reports preferences that vary by sex, culture and context rather than a single preferred colouring [4][5][6].

paras: The term appears in forum thread titles that frame a story or observation as a revelation, with members adding their own anecdotes and photos in replies [1]. A typical example on looksmax.org is a poster who overheard a woman praising her tanned, green-eyed, dark-haired boyfriend, titled as a "brutal medpill"; replies add jokes, counter-examples and questions about whether green eyes matter [1].

Threads of this kind sit within the community's wider discussion of how ethnicity, colouring and phenotype are perceived. Some such threads contain ethnic generalisations and heated language, and the wiki documents the term without endorsing any of those generalisations.

The pill metaphor comes from The Matrix, in which Morpheus offers Neo a blue pill to stay in comfortable ignorance or a red pill to see the underlying reality. The manosphere adopted red pill and popularised it through the subreddit r/TheRedPill, created in 2012, where it describes accepting a set of claims about gender and society [2].

Wikipedia describes the black pill as having developed on incel forums as a more nihilistic offshoot that holds that appearance largely determines outcomes in dating and that unattractive men cannot escape the bottom of the hierarchy; the Anti-Defamation League is cited as distinguishing red-pilled incels, who think they can improve their prospects, from black-pilled ones who think they cannot [3]. Looksmaxxing itself is described as growing out of those communities and spreading through TikTok in the 2020s [7]. Medpill is one of many later labels formed on the same pattern; the plain-text label tells readers a single claim is being presented as a hard truth, and it has no formal definition outside forum use.

Proponents cite anecdotes, such as a woman praising a tanned, dark-haired partner, and observations about well-known people to argue that fair colouring is not the only preferred look and that darker colouring is underrated [1]. Some members connect the idea to practical choices: keeping a tan, avoiding looking pale or washed out, or choosing darker hair.

Other forum members, in the same threads, respond that such cases are individual and that preferences vary, and ask whether the cited person's eye colour or other features, rather than complexion, are doing the work [1]. Outside the forums, researchers who study attractiveness describe preferences that differ between individuals and populations (see Research and expert views).

Because medpill is a belief label, practice consists mostly of thread discussion. Where members act on it, the usual levers are skin tone (sunless tanning products, sun exposure or tanning beds), hair colour and styling, and clothing colours that suit darker complexions. Dermatology and public health bodies describe these differently: Wikipedia's article on indoor tanning notes that UV radiation is a Group 1 carcinogen in the World Health Organization's cancer agency classification and cites meta-analyses reporting higher melanoma risk among tanning-device users, while sunless products such as dihydroxyacetone (DHA) are described as approved by the US FDA for external application but not for use around the eyes, lips or by inhalation [8][9].

No published study has tested the claim as it is phrased in these forums, that Mediterranean men outperform Nordic men. Nearby research addresses components of it. In experiments led by Ian Stephen and David Perrett at St Andrews and Bristol, participants preferred skin coloured by carotenoids from fruit and vegetables to skin coloured by suntan, and a 2013 Biology Letters study by Lefevre, Perrett and colleagues found that carotenoid colouration raised face attractiveness while the same colour changes had no comparable effect on scrambled non-face images, which the authors interpreted as a signal of current health [5][6].

For hair colour, a 2015 study by Janif, Brooks and Dixson in Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology had 1,494 women and 658 men rate female face portraits and found that men rated blond hair highest followed by brown, women rated brown highest followed by blond, and both rated red lowest; the authors reported no evidence that rarity increased attractiveness [4]. That study concerned women's hair and does not bear on male colouring directly. Attractiveness researchers more generally report that preferences vary by individual, culture and era, and the wiki does not treat the medpill claim as either established or ruled out.

The idea itself has no direct physical risk. Tanning by UV exposure is associated with documented skin-cancer and skin-ageing risks [8]. Community discussion of the term sometimes shades into ethnic generalisation; Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article records criticism from researchers, physicians and journalists that appearance-ranking culture can be judgemental and linked to body dysmorphia [7].
No studies found. Related research on skin colour, tanning and hair colour is summarised above.
